Figure 113: Frequency bands received and transmitted by the Fairphone (Gen. 6), with band edges according to 3GPP. FDD bands show uplink (UL, phone transmits) and downlink (DL, phone receives) separately; TDD bands use the same frequencies for both. The shaded areas are the band groups LB, MB, HB, and UHB used in this appendix. Note the logarithmic frequency axis.





In the RF front-end, the bands are sorted into band groups; in this appendix we use low band (LB, 617 MHz to 960 MHz), mid band (MB, 1452 MHz to 2200 MHz), high band (HB, 2300 MHz to 2690 MHz), and ultra-high band (UHB, 3300 MHz to 5000 MHz). Within a band group, LNAs, PAs, and antennas can be shared, as their relative bandwidth is moderate (e.g., 44 % for LB and 41 % for MB). A single amplifier covering all bands from 617 MHz to 5 GHz would be much harder to match (see the Bode-Fano limit in Section 4.1) and would let all out-of-band signals pass.
Below 2.7 GHz, most bands are FDD, while the TDD bands (B38 to B42, n77, n78) are located at higher frequencies, as already noted in Table 4. In FDD, the receiver has to be protected from the strong TX signal of the same phone by a duplexer (see Section 3.5). The difficulty of building this duplexer is set by the duplex gap \(f_\mathrm{gap}\) between the upper edge of the uplink and the lower edge of the downlink (or vice versa). Within the gap, the filter has to transition from its passband to a high attenuation. Using the definition of the filter quality factor \(Q = f_\mathrm{c} / \Delta f\) from Section 3, the resonators of the duplexer need a quality factor of at least
\[
Q_\mathrm{min} = \frac{f_\mathrm{c}}{f_\mathrm{gap}},
\tag{83}\]
which is evaluated for all FDD bands of the phone in Figure 114. Many bands have a duplex gap of only 10 MHz to 20 MHz, so that \(Q_\mathrm{min}\) is close to 100, while a realistic filter needs resonators with a \(Q\) that is an order of magnitude higher to achieve a steep transition with low insertion loss. On-chip \(LC\) filters with a \(Q\) of 10 to 20 are hopeless here, which is why every FDD band needs its own acoustic (SAW or BAW) duplexer. Only bands 4 and 66, whose uplink and downlink are separated by more than 300 MHz, would be uncritical.








Figure 114: Duplex gap \(f_\mathrm{gap}\) between uplink and downlink (left) and the resulting lower bound \(Q_\mathrm{min} = f_\mathrm{c} / f_\mathrm{gap}\) of the filter quality factor (right) for the FDD bands of the Fairphone (Gen. 6). The shaded areas mark the \(Q\) of on-chip \(LC\) filters (10 to 20) and of acoustic SAW/BAW resonators (thousands, see Section 3).











NoteNumber of Filters in a Phone



Every FDD band needs a duplexer, every band used for receive diversity and MIMO needs additional receive filters, and the GNSS and Wi-Fi paths need their own filters as well. This is why a phone contains a large number of acoustic filters, and why a new band cannot simply be added in software.

title: Radio-Frequency Integrated Circuits
text:
11.3 Antennas
The phone uses 11 antenna feeds. A large number of antennas is needed for three reasons:

MIMO: For 4×4 downlink MIMO in the mid, high, and ultra-high bands, four independent receive paths per band have to be connected to four different antennas (named primary RX (PRX), diversity RX (DRX), PRX MIMO, and DRX MIMO). The low bands use 2×2 MIMO, as the antennas for long wavelengths (about 40 cm at 750 MHz) are large and difficult to fit into a phone.
Concurrent operation: Cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and GNSS work at the same time.
Sounding reference signals (SRS): In the TDD bands 41 and n77/n78, the phone transmits a pilot signal on each of its receive antennas in turn, so that the base station can measure the full channel matrix for beamforming. This requires switches that connect the transmitter to every receive antenna.

Most antennas serve several band groups, which are separated by diplexers (two bands) or triplexers (three bands). For example, one antenna is shared by the B32 downlink, GNSS L1, and Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz: a diplexer splits it into 704 MHz to 1610 MHz and 2400 MHz to 5950 MHz, and a triplexer separates the B32 and GNSS L1 signals afterwards.
The two antennas that carry the LB transmitters are equipped with antenna tuners. The impedance of a small phone antenna depends strongly on frequency and on the environment (e.g., the hand of the user), and an antenna tuner (a network of switched capacitors and inductors, see Section 4.1) adapts the matching network to the band in use and to changing conditions. This is especially important in the low bands, where the antenna is electrically small compared to the wavelength.

title: Radio-Frequency Integrated Circuits
text:
11.4 Cellular Transceiver SDR735
The SDR735 is a highly integrated multi-band transceiver. No datasheet is public, but its pinout in the schematics (Fairphone B.V. 2025) already tells a lot about its architecture:

Receivers: four groups of RF inputs for the primary (P), diversity (D), primary MIMO (PM), and diversity MIMO (DM) receive paths, each with several inputs for the different band groups. These are the four receive paths needed for 4×4 downlink MIMO.
Transmitters: two transmit chains (TX0 and TX1), each with six RF outputs for the different band groups.
Feedback receiver: one input (FBRX) that measures the transmitted signal (see Section 11.6.2).
GNSS receiver: two inputs, for the L1 and L5 bands.
Digital interfaces: the QLink interface to the SoC and the RFFE buses and GPIOs that control the front-end.
Unused features: outputs for envelope-tracking DACs (ETDAC0, ETDAC1), which are not connected in the Fairphone (see Section 11.6.1).

There are no IF filters between the front-end and the RFIC in the schematics; the RF inputs and outputs of the RFIC connect directly to the front-end modules. This is consistent with the direct-conversion architecture of Section 3.1, where the channel selection is done by analog low-pass filters and digital filters on the RFIC. A simplified receive path from antenna to digital I/Q interface is shown in Figure 115.








Figure 115: Simplified primary receive path of the Fairphone (Gen. 6) for band 1 or band 3, from the antenna to the digital I/Q interface. The I and Q paths of the direct-conversion receiver are drawn as one; the Q path uses a second mixer driven by the LO shifted by 90°.





The synthesizers of such a transceiver have to generate LO frequencies for all supported bands, from 617 MHz (B71) up to 3.8 GHz (n78), a ratio of more than 6:1. As discussed in Section 6.6, an LC VCO only achieves a limited tuning range, so the LO is usually derived from a VCO followed by frequency dividers. A divide-by-2 stage is needed anyway to generate quadrature LO signals (see Section 5.5.3), and further divide-by-2 stages extend the range downwards by octaves. Then the VCOs of a synthesizer have to cover one octave together. If a single VCO tunes from \(f_\mathrm{c} (1 - \mathrm{TR})\) to \(f_\mathrm{c} (1 + \mathrm{TR})\), the number of VCOs needed to cover one octave is
\[
N_\mathrm{VCO} \geq \frac{\ln 2}{\ln \left( \frac{1 + \mathrm{TR}}{1 - \mathrm{TR}} \right)}.
\tag{84}\]
For a tuning range of ±15 % (TR = 0.15), which is ambitious for a low-phase-noise LC VCO, we get \(N_\mathrm{VCO} \geq 2.3\), i.e., three VCOs per synthesizer. As an FDD transceiver with MIMO and two transmitters needs several synthesizers running at the same time, a multi-band RFIC contains many VCOs.
The RFIC uses several supply voltages (0.8 V, 0.875 V, 1.2 V, and 1.8 V), provided by the power management ICs (Fairphone B.V. 2025).

title: Radio-Frequency Integrated Circuits
text:
11.5 Receive Path
In the Fairphone, the LNAs are not placed in the RFIC but in separate LNA modules: one for the LB primary receivers (QLN5020), one for the MB and HB primary receivers (QLN5040), and one for the LB, MB, and HB diversity receivers (QLN5030). The n77/n78 receivers use separate modules that combine LNAs with the PA (QPM2980) or with the diversity receivers (QDM3980). Each LNA module contains several LNAs, each with an input switch (SPnT) that selects one of several band filters, and an output multiplexer that routes the amplified signals to the RFIC inputs (see Figure 115); this reduces the routing complexity on the PCB.
External LNAs improve the noise figure of the receiver. All losses between the antenna and the first amplifier add directly to the noise figure of the receiver (a passive component with loss \(L\) has a noise factor \(F = L\), see Section 2.3.3), and in the Fairphone the signal passes through a diplexer, an antenna switch, and a filter before it reaches the LNA module. An LNA directly after the filter fixes the noise figure early in the chain, so that the noise of the RFIC matters less, as the example in Note 13 shows.






Note 13: Noise Figure of the Receive Path



We assume (as typical values, not taken from datasheets) a total loss of \(L\) = 2.6 dB in front of the LNA (diplexer 0.4 dB, antenna switch 0.7 dB, and filter 1.5 dB), an external LNA with NF = 1 dB and a gain of \(G\) = 18 dB, and an RFIC with NF = 6 dB. With the Friis formula (Equation 22) and \(F = L\) for the passive components, the receiver has a noise factor of
\[
F = L \left( F_\mathrm{LNA} + \frac{F_\mathrm{RFIC} - 1}{G} \right) = 1.82 \cdot \left( 1.26 + \frac{3.98 - 1}{63.1} \right) = 2.38,
\]
i.e., a noise figure of 3.8 dB. Without the external LNA, the noise figure would be \(2.6\,\text{dB} + 6\,\text{dB} = 8.6\,\text{dB}\), which would reduce the sensitivity (Equation 24) by almost 5 dB.


For the GNSS receivers, the situation is even more critical, as the satellite signals arrive far below the thermal noise floor. Here, each band (L1 and L5) uses an external LNA between two SAW filters. The first filter protects the LNA from the strong cellular and Wi-Fi signals of the phone itself, and the second filter provides additional out-of-band filtering before further amplification.

title: Radio-Frequency Integrated Circuits
text:
11.6 Transmit Path
The transmit path is shown in Figure 116. The RFIC generates the modulated RF signal with a direct-conversion transmitter. This signal is amplified to the required output power by one of two multimode PA modules (MMPA) for the LB, MB, and HB bands, which contain PAs for the three band groups together with band switches. A dedicated PA module (QPA2625) is used for GSM, and the n77/n78 band has its own PA in the QPM2980 module. The PA output passes through the duplexer of the active band, an antenna switch, and a directional coupler to the antenna.








Figure 116: Simplified transmit path of the Fairphone (Gen. 6) for band 1 or band 3. The supply of the PA comes from an average power tracker; a directional coupler between the antenna switch and the antenna feeds a sample of the TX signal back to the feedback receiver (FBRX) of the RFIC. The I and Q paths of the direct-conversion transmitter are drawn as one.





The maximum output power at the antenna connector is 23 dBm (power class 3) for most bands and 26 dBm (power class 2, high-power UE) for bands 41 and n78 (3GPP 2026a, 2026b).

11.6.1 Average Power Tracking
A phone transmits at full power only at the cell edge; closer to the base station, the output power is reduced by the power control. With a fixed supply voltage, the efficiency of a linear PA drops quickly at reduced output power (see Section 8.1). The Fairphone therefore supplies each of the two MMPAs from its own dc-dc converter (QET3930), whose outputs are labeled as APT supplies (VPA0_APT and VPA1_APT) in the schematics (Fairphone B.V. 2025). With APT, the PA supply voltage is adjusted to the average output power of the current transmission slot. This average power tracking (APT) is a simple form of the supply modulation discussed with Class G and Class H in Section 8.3.
To quantify the benefit, we model an ideal class-B PA. For an RF amplitude \(a\) at the drain and a load resistance \(R\), the output power is \(P_\mathrm{out} = a^2 / (2R)\) and the dc power drawn from the supply \(V_\mathrm{DD}\) is \(P_\mathrm{dc} = 2 V_\mathrm{DD} a / (\pi R)\). For a modulated signal with a varying envelope \(a(t)\), the average drain efficiency becomes
\[
\eta = \frac{\pi}{4} \frac{\mathrm{E}\{a^2\}}{\mathrm{E}\{V_\mathrm{DD} \, a\}},
\tag{85}\]
which reaches the class-B limit \(\pi / 4\) only if \(V_\mathrm{DD}\) follows the envelope \(a(t)\) at every instant. For an OFDM signal, the I and Q components are approximately Gaussian, so the envelope is Rayleigh distributed, with \(\mathrm{E}\{a^2\} = 2 \sigma^2\) and \(\mathrm{E}\{a\} = \sigma \sqrt{\pi / 2}\). If the supply is set to the envelope peak \(a_\mathrm{pk} = \sigma \sqrt{2\,\text{PAPR}}\), Equation 85 yields
\[
\eta_\mathrm{APT} = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2 \sqrt{\text{PAPR}}},
\tag{86}\]
independent of the output power. For a PAPR of 8 dB, this gives 35 %. With a fixed supply, the supply is set by the peak at maximum output power, and the efficiency falls by 10 dB for every 10 dB of output power back-off, while APT keeps the efficiency constant as long as the dc-dc converter can lower its output voltage. Figure 117 compares fixed supply, APT, and envelope tracking (ET), where the supply follows the envelope instantaneously.








Figure 117: Average drain efficiency of an ideal class-B PA amplifying an OFDM signal (Rayleigh-distributed envelope, supply sized for a PAPR of 8 dB) versus average output power, for a fixed supply, average power tracking (APT), and envelope tracking (ET). The fixed supply is sized for the maximum output power of 23 dBm (power class 3); the tracking supply cannot go below 0.5 V for a 3.8 V battery. The losses of the dc-dc converter are not included.





At 13 dBm output power, i.e., 10 dB below maximum, APT improves the drain efficiency from 11 % to 35 %. ET more than doubles the efficiency at high output power, but requires a tracking supply with a bandwidth of several times the signal bandwidth, which is difficult and power hungry for the wide channels of LTE and 5G NR. The SDR735 has outputs to control an envelope tracker (ETDAC0 and ETDAC1), but in the Fairphone, they are not connected; the phone relies on APT.


11.6.2 Feedback Receiver
The transmit power has to be controlled accurately (the maximum output power, for example, has a tolerance of about ±2 dB (3GPP 2026a)), and the transmitter has to meet the requirements for the error vector magnitude (EVM, see Equation 30) and the adjacent channel leakage. As the gain of the PA depends on temperature, supply voltage, frequency, and antenna impedance, the phone measures its own output: a directional coupler between the antenna switch and the antenna couples a small part of the transmitted signal to the feedback receiver (FBRX) input of the RFIC, via a switch that selects the coupler of the active transmitter. A feedback receiver allows the digital baseband to compare the transmitted with the intended signal, which can be used for closed-loop power control, for the calibration of I/Q imbalance and LO leakage of the transmitter (see Section 3.1), and for digital predistortion of the PA (see Section 8.5).


11.6.3 Dual Uplink and Self-Interference
For bands 1 and 3, the Fairphone uses a quadplexer instead of two separate duplexers (Fairphone B.V. 2025): a filter with one antenna port and four ports for B1 TX, B1 RX, B3 TX, and B3 RX. A quadplexer allows both bands to be connected to the same antenna at the same time, as needed for carrier aggregation of B1 and B3, possibly with an uplink in both bands (dual uplink). When two transmit signals pass through a nonlinear component (the PA output stages, the antenna switch, or the quadplexer itself), they generate harmonics and intermodulation products (see Section 2.2). In the classification of self-interference mechanisms of (Sadjina et al. 2020), this is TX-to-RX crosstalk: the interferer is generated from the phone’s own transmit signals and reaches its receivers through the shared front-end, where the TX-to-RX isolation of the quadplexer and of the antenna switch is finite (see also Section 9.1). Figure 118 shows where these products of B1 and B3 fall.








Figure 118: Harmonics and intermodulation products \(|m f_\mathrm{B3} + n f_\mathrm{B1}|\) of a dual uplink in bands 1 and 3 (\(f_\mathrm{B1}\) = 1920 MHz to 1980 MHz, \(f_\mathrm{B3}\) = 1710 MHz to 1785 MHz). The shaded columns are the receive bands of the phone; the parts of a product that fall into a receive band are drawn in red, and the affected receive bands are listed next to each product.





Several products land in receive bands of the same phone:

The third-order product \(2 f_\mathrm{B1} - f_\mathrm{B3}\) (2055 MHz to 2250 MHz) covers the entire B1 downlink. This is the most critical case, as the phone has to receive in B1 while it transmits the two signals that create the interferer.
The third-order product \(2 f_\mathrm{B3} - f_\mathrm{B1}\) (1440 MHz to 1650 MHz) falls into B32 and into the GNSS L1 band.
The second harmonics and the second-order sum product fall into the n77/n78 bands, and higher-order products into the Wi-Fi 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands.

How linear do the components have to be? In dual uplink, the maximum output power of 23 dBm is shared by the two carriers, so each carrier has about 20 dBm. If the IM3 product shall stay below -110 dBm, i.e., about 7 dB below the noise floor of -103 dBm of a receiver with a 5 MHz channel and NF = 4 dB (see Equation 24), solving Equation 15 for the IIP3 of the components after the PAs gives
\[
\text{IIP3} = P_\mathrm{in} + \frac{P_\mathrm{in} - P_\mathrm{IM3}}{2} = 20\,\text{dBm} + \frac{20 - (-110)}{2}\,\text{dB} = 85\,\text{dBm},
\]
a value that is extremely hard to met by real switches and filters. 3GPP therefore allows a maximum sensitivity degradation (MSD) for band combinations whose intermodulation products fall into an own receive band (3GPP 2026a), and the front-end designer minimizes the degradation with highly linear switches and filters and by keeping the two TX signals isolated from each other for as long as possible (e.g., using different antennas).
A complementary approach is self-interference cancellation in the receiver (Sadjina et al. 2020). Unlike an external blocker, the interferer here is created from signals the phone knows exactly: its own TX baseband samples. An adaptive model of the nonlinear coupling path, driven by the two TX signals, can therefore reproduce the IM3 product in the digital baseband and subtract it from the received signal. As the coupling path changes with antenna impedance, temperature, and output power, the model parameters are estimated continuously (e.g., with LMS-type adaptive algorithms). Cancellation relaxes the linearity requirements of the front-end, at the cost of additional digital signal processing. Whether such a technique is used in the Fairphone is unknown.
This is a good example of the self-interference problems discussed in Section 9: in a multi-band radio, the strongest interferer is often the own transmitter.

title: Radio-Frequency Integrated Circuits
text:
11.7 Wi-Fi and Bluetooth
Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are handled by the WCN6755, which is connected to the SoC via PCIe (Fairphone B.V. 2025). In contrast to the cellular radio, the WCN6755 integrates the PAs on chip. Wi-Fi uses TDD (see Table 4), so a switch instead of a duplexer separates TX and RX. For 2×2 MIMO, the WCN6755 has two independent RF chains per band, which are connected to separate antennas. Bluetooth shares the 2.4 GHz RF ports with Wi-Fi (the pins are labeled WLBT), so Wi-Fi and Bluetooth at 2.4 GHz use the same antenna paths.

title: Transceivers
text:
3.1 Direct-Conversion Transceiver

Nowadays, the various small-signal RF functions for receive and transmit are integrated into so-called transceivers (TRX). A TRX is a device that can both transmit and receive signals, and is usually called an “RFIC”. While high monolithic integration is certainly the norm for radio-frequency devices intended for standards like Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, cellular, etc., it is increasingly used also for mm-wave frequencies for applications like automotive radar and 5G cellular.
Typically, TRX include components like amplifiers, mixers, filters, oscillators, and phase-locked loops. When digital interfaces are used for the baseband I/Q data, also functions like analog-to-digital conversion (ADC) and digital-to-analog conversion (DAC) are integrated together with digital signal processing (DSP) blocks and potentially high-speed interfaces (because for wide bandwidths the I/Q sample rate can get quite high).
In these notes we will focus on the RF part of the TRX, which is responsible for the upconversion of baseband or intermediate frequency (IF) signals to the desired transmit frequency during transmission, and the downconversion of received signals from the carrier frequency to baseband or IF during reception. For filters, low-frequency amplifiers, ADCs, DACs, and DSP blocks we refer to related courses and literature, for example our analog circuit design course.

title: Transceivers
text:
3.2 Modulation and Demodulation

As can be seen in Figure 19, this generic architecture can be adapted in various ways. Generally, the amplifier gains are adjustable to adapt to different signal levels. If adaptive channel bandwidths are to be supported, the corner frequencies of the low-pass filters (LPF) can be adjusted, as well as (optionally) the sampling rate of the ADCs and DACs. The local oscillator (LO) frequency is generated by a phase-locked loop (PLL) synthesizer, which can be tuned to the desired carrier frequency. In case of frequency-division duplex (FDD) operation, two PLLs are used to generate the TX and RX LO frequencies, which are separated by the duplex distance \(f_\mathrm{dpx}\). In time-division duplex (TDD) operation, a single PLL is sufficient, supplying the LO signal to both RX and TX.
The modem (short for modulator-demodulator) that is shown in Figure 19 is responsible for the digital baseband processing, including functions like channel coding/decoding, modulation/demodulation, equalization, error correction, encryption/decryption, and framing/timing. The modem is usually implemented as a digital System-on-Chip (SoC) consisting of (multiple) CPUs, DSPs, and fixed-function blocks for time-critical processing. For an in-depth discussion we recommend (Sklar and Harris 2020) or (Molisch 2022).

3.4 Direct-Conversion Architecture

Fundamentally, the choice of filter technology is a trade-off between performance, size, cost, power handling, and flexibility. In most cases, a combination of different filter technologies is used to achieve the desired performance.

title: Transceivers
text:
3.5 Duplexing

Nowadays there exist good design techniques to mitigate these disadvantages. However, in some cases (for example very high linearity requirements, or very high frequencies) other architectures like low-IF or super-heterodyne may be preferable.

title: Transceivers
text:
3.6 Specialty Architectures

Regardless of whether two antennas or a circulator are used, the isolation between the TX and RX paths is always finite (typically only in the range of 15 dB to 20 dB for a circulator). As a consequence, a large fraction of the own (and strong) TX signal leaks directly into the sensitive RX port. Practical FD systems therefore require additional self-interference cancellation (also called leakage cancellation), performed in the RF/analog and/or digital domain, to suppress this residual TX leakage below the RX noise floor (Sadjina et al. 2020).

title: Transceivers
text:
3.7 I/Q Imbalance

Despite the reduced architecture, digital amplitude-shift-keying (ASK) or on-off-keying (OOK) can be used. If the receiver is able to discriminate between frequencies (e.g., by using two RF filters with a power detector each), also frequency-shift-keying (FSK) can be used.

title: Low Noise Amplifiers
text:
4.1 Impedance Matching

The LNA as a building block is shown in Figure 31. It is usually designed for a specific frequency band, e.g., the 2.4 GHz ISM band or the 5 GHz WLAN band, and is typically designed for a specific impedance, e.g., 50 Ω, which is the standard impedance for RF systems. Impedance matching is usually mandated at the input; the output impedance matching is only required if the output of the LNA goes off-chip; if it is kept on-chip, impedance matching is often not needed. The LNA is also designed to be sufficiently linear, i.e., to not introduce significant distortion to the amplified signal; however, compared to the noise requirements, linearity is often less critical.

If these spurs are inside the channel bandwidth, they cause EVM degradation and may violate spectral mask requirements.

text:
7.3 All-Digital PLL

Note that inside the PLL loop bandwidth the reference phase noise is multiplied by \(N^2\) in power, i.e., \(20 \log_{10}(N)\) in dB, as the PLL output frequency is \(N\) times the reference frequency. In Figure 84, \(N = 100\) and a reference phase noise of -140 dBc/Hz is used. Large values of \(N\) can significantly increase the reference phase noise contribution at the PLL output, which is why low phase noise references are essential for high-performance PLLs.

title: Phase-Locked Loops
text:
7.4 Fractional-N PLL

It has to be noted that while an ADPLL seems conceptually simpler than an analog PLL, the design of high-performance TDCs and DCOs can be quite complex and requires careful consideration of quantization noise, linearity, and power consumption. Coupling effects between different circuit blocks can also introduce unwanted spurs and phase noise folding in the ADPLL output. Therefore, while ADPLLs offer many advantages, they also present unique design challenges that must be addressed to achieve adequate performance.

title: MASH Modulator (3rd Order)
text:
Import Libraries

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

title: MASH Modulator (3rd Order)
text:
MASH Modulator Class
The MASH (Multi-stAge noise SHaping) modulator consists of three cascaded 1st-order stages with digital noise cancellation logic.

class MASHModulator:
    """3rd order MASH (Multi-stAge noise SHaping) modulator"""
    
    def __init__(self):
        """Initialize the 3-stage MASH modulator."""
        # Three 1st order stages
        self.integrator1 = 0.0
        self.integrator2 = 0.0
        self.integrator3 = 0.0
        
        # Storage for digital cancellation logic (need 2 delays)
        self.y1_prev = 0
        self.y1_prev2 = 0
        self.y2_prev = 0
        self.y2_prev2 = 0
        self.y3_prev = 0
        self.y3_prev2 = 0
    
    def reset(self):
        """Reset all states to zero"""
        self.integrator1 = 0.0
        self.integrator2 = 0.0
        self.integrator3 = 0.0
        self.y1_prev = 0
        self.y1_prev2 = 0
        self.y2_prev = 0
        self.y2_prev2 = 0
        self.y3_prev = 0
        self.y3_prev2 = 0
    
    def step(self, input_value):
        """
        Perform one step of MASH modulation.
        
        Parameters:
        -----------
        input_value : float
            Input signal value (0-1)
        
        Returns:
        --------
        tuple
            (combined_output, y1, y2, y3) - combined output and individual stage outputs
        """
        # Stage 1: 1st order modulator with input signal
        self.integrator1 += input_value
        y1 = 1 if self.integrator1 >= 1.0 else 0
        e1 = self.integrator1 - y1  # Quantization error
        self.integrator1 = e1  # Store error for next iteration
        
        # Stage 2: 1st order modulator fed with quantization error from stage 1
        self.integrator2 += e1
        y2 = 1 if self.integrator2 >= 1.0 else 0
        e2 = self.integrator2 - y2
        self.integrator2 = e2
        
        # Stage 3: 1st order modulator fed with quantization error from stage 2
        self.integrator3 += e2
        y3 = 1 if self.integrator3 >= 1.0 else 0
        e3 = self.integrator3 - y3
        self.integrator3 = e3
        
        # Digital noise cancellation logic for MASH 1-1-1
        # Output = Y1 + (1-z^-1)*Y2 + (1-z^-1)^2*Y3
        # Expanding (1-z^-1)^2 = 1 - 2*z^-1 + z^-2:
        # Output = Y1 + Y2 - Y2[z^-1] + Y3 - 2*Y3[z^-1] + Y3[z^-2]
        
        combined = y1 + (y2 - self.y2_prev) + (y3 - 2*self.y3_prev + self.y3_prev2)
        
        # Update delay elements
        self.y1_prev2 = self.y1_prev
        self.y1_prev = y1
        
        self.y2_prev2 = self.y2_prev
        self.y2_prev = y2
        
        self.y3_prev2 = self.y3_prev
        self.y3_prev = y3
        
        return combined, y1, y2, y3
    
    def modulate(self, input_value, length, dither_amplitude=0.0, seed=None):
        """
        Generate MASH modulated sequence.
        
        Parameters:
        -----------
        input_value : float
            Constant input value (0-1)
        length : int
            Length of output sequence
        dither_amplitude : float
            Peak dither amplitude added to input (uniform in [-A, +A])
        seed : int or None
            RNG seed for reproducible dithering
        
        Returns:
        --------
        tuple
            (combined_output, y1, y2, y3) - arrays of combined and individual outputs
            Combined output range: -3 to +4 (multi-bit output)
        """
        self.reset()
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        combined_output = np.zeros(length)
        y1_output = np.zeros(length)
        y2_output = np.zeros(length)
        y3_output = np.zeros(length)
        
        for i in range(length):
            dither = rng.uniform(-dither_amplitude, dither_amplitude) if dither_amplitude > 0 else 0.0
            combined, y1, y2, y3 = self.step(input_value + dither)
            combined_output[i] = combined
            y1_output[i] = y1
            y2_output[i] = y2
            y3_output[i] = y3
        
        return combined_output, y1_output, y2_output, y3_output
